teaser: A stack of wheat taller than a house, and not one stroke of black in its shadow.
review_notes:
Stack height of 15 to 20 feet follows the Art Institute of Chicago's description.
The story that Monet paid the farmer to leave the stacks standing over the winter is traditional; check.
Blanche Hoschedé and the wheelbarrow of canvases: widely repeated account.
Series count (about 25 canvases, 15 shown in May 1891, sold within days) to confirm.
2019 Sotheby's sale of another stack painting for $110.7 million.
AIC owns six paintings from the series; Bertha Palmer as early Chicago buyer.
Kandinsky anecdote (Moscow, 1896) comes from his own memoirs.

lesson.text: The canvas is one meter wide and 60 centimeters high, about 3 feet by 2. The thing painted on it was far bigger: a stack like the one on the right stood 15 to 20 feet tall (roughly 5 to 6 meters). A grown man would barely reach the point where the sloping roof begins.

People often call these haystacks. They are not hay. Each one is a pile of wheat, bundled stalk by stalk with the grain still on it, then capped with a thatched cone to keep the rain out. The stack was a storehouse. It waited in the field for months until a threshing machine came through the village to separate grain from straw.

These stacks stood in a field right beside Monet's house in Giverny, a short walk from his door. They belonged to a neighboring farmer, and the story goes that Monet paid him to leave them standing through the winter so the painting could go on.

So why paint a farmer's storehouse about 25 times? Because Monet was not really painting wheat. Here the sun is low and sits behind the stacks, off to the right. That puts the sides facing you in shadow. Now see what he does with that shadow.

lesson.title: A shadow made of color
lesson.text: Evening light comes from behind and from the right. Follow it across the canvas.

spots.title: Where the sun is going
spots.text: The sky turns from pale blue to yellow-green and pink on this side. The sun itself is outside the frame, but every color in the picture answers to this corner.

spots.title: The dark side
spots.text: This face of the stack gets no direct sun. Monet builds it from brick red, orange, violet and rose. There is no black and no brown anywhere in it.

spots.title: The small stack
spots.text: Farther away, the second stack is cooler and pinker, with a violet band at its base. Its outline melts into the field, as things do when you look toward a low sun.

spots.title: The ground
spots.text: The stubble field is a weave of pink, lilac and green dashes. Light bouncing off the sky fills the shade with color.

lesson.text: For Monet a shadow was never an absence of light. It was light of another color, and he painted it with the same bright pigments as the sunlit parts.

That kind of light lasts only a few minutes. When Monet began in the late summer of 1890, he thought two canvases would do: one for sun, one for gray weather. The light kept changing faster than he could work. He ended up with a canvas for each effect, switching from one to the next as the hour moved on, and touching them up later in the studio.
His stepdaughter Blanche Hoschedé, a painter herself, is said to have pushed the unfinished canvases out to the field in a wheelbarrow, handing Monet a fresh one each time the light shifted.
With so much attention on the two stacks, the strip between them is easy to skip. Yet this is not an empty field in the middle of nowhere. People live just behind it.
A farm building hides among the trees. Can you spot its roof?

spots.title: A rooftop
spots.text: A small pink triangle with a pale wall below it: a house or barn at the edge of the village. Its sloping roof repeats, in miniature, the cone of the stacks.

lesson.text: That roof ties the stacks to the people who built them. Behind it runs a line of trees and blue hills that Monet keeps soft and level, so the big cone on the right can break through it and rise into the sky. A plain farm object ends up with the presence of a monument.
In May 1891 Monet showed fifteen of the stacks together in a Paris gallery. They sold out within days. In 2019 a single canvas from the series went at auction for 110.7 million dollars.

The Art Institute of Chicago owns six paintings from the series, more than any other museum, because Chicago collectors bought them almost as soon as they were dry. Seeing several together is the real point: same field, same stacks, a different hour each time.

A young Russian lawyer saw one of these stacks in a Moscow exhibition in 1896 and could not work out what it showed. He was annoyed, then haunted by it. His name was Wassily Kandinsky, and he later became a pioneer of abstract painting.
Next time you are outdoors as the sun goes down, check the shady side of a wall, a car, a tree. Is it gray? Or is it, as Monet insisted, full of violet and red?

quiz.question: What are the stacks actually made of?
options: Bundled wheat with the grain still on it
Straw left over after the harvest
quiz.explanation: They are stores of unthreshed wheat, capped with thatch against the rain.

quiz.question: Where is the sun in this picture?
options: Low, behind the stacks and to the right
quiz.explanation: The light comes from behind and from the right, leaving the near sides in shadow.

quiz.question: Which colors does Monet use for the shaded face of the large stack?
quiz.explanation: He paints shadow as colored light, without black or brown.

quiz.question: What small detail sits between the two stacks?
options: The roof of a farm building
quiz.explanation: A pink rooftop shows among the trees, echoing the cone of the stacks.

quiz.question: Which future abstract painter was struck by one of these stacks in Moscow?
quiz.explanation: Kandinsky saw one in 1896 and did not recognize the subject at first.

facts.text: Monet first planned to paint only two canvases of the stacks.
facts.explanation: He expected one for sun and one for gray weather, then the changing light multiplied them.

facts.text: The stacks stood in a remote field far from any village.
facts.explanation: They stood next to Monet's house in Giverny, and a farm roof is visible between them.

facts.text: The fifteen stacks Monet exhibited in 1891 sold within days.
facts.explanation: The Paris show was an immediate commercial success.
